Formal proof of correctness on a large, real-world program is hard. Very, very hard. And that's assuming you do it right, with a solid, non-moving target. AFAIK, software isn't written in a way where this is easily facilitated. This is a serious problem for all involved - most major programs are constantly evolving and expanding, and many classes of software are rather useless if they aren't. Furthermore, many require, by virtue of their very function, the use of external code within them. Although this can all be mitigated, this is just plain hard, REALLY hard, to actually ensure, and you would have to continuously add in new parts, and presumably do some sort of regression testing as well. While it may be possible to do this for a few key, critical portions of the code, there's plenty of other code that can still be broken in one way or another in non-critical sections, which means that a certification like this is of somewhat limited value.

I'll try to make this a little more ELI5 than the other posts.

4 kids are in the playground talking about how cool it is that Santa is coming. One kid comes to join them but disagrees as he suspects that Santa is not real and that it might be his parents. The other kids are annoyed by this suggestion and tell him to leave. Another child comes over but this time exclaims that he also thinks it's great that Santa is coming and so is welcomed into the discussion by the other children. By behaving like this the children maintain the belief that Santa is real even in the face of evidence/opinions to the contrary because they have created an echo-chamber: a space where their pre-existing views are simply repeated back to them.

Of course the "echo-chamber" (the group of kids in the above example) can be right, or wrong, or just debating an abstract subjective. What matters is that they maintain the status quo (they keep the opinion that already exists as the dominant one) because they react negatively to perspectives that call their views into question.

The concern about echo-chambers is not that they always hold the right or wrong view but that if they do hold the wrong view it can be very hard to change the opinion of the group at large.

In the case of this site: someone might argue that many Voat users have similar perspective (a lot of people came here for the same reasons). So this might make them more likely to more readily reject views that are opposed to their pre-existing perspectives.

In reality this is true of every community. It's difficult to overcome both at a group and individual level without a lot of work. Personally, I think the restrictions on the downvote button does go some way to help with this though of course it can't solve the issue.
